result.title: A six-month periodic fasting reduces microalbuminuria and improves metabolic control in patients with type 2 diabetes and diabetic nephropathy: a randomized controlled study

knowledge_units.context_summary: A randomized controlled study assessed the effects of a six-month fasting-mimicking diet versus a Mediterranean diet on patients with type 2 diabetes and diabetic nephropathy. The study found that the fasting-mimicking diet reduced microalbuminuria and HOMA-IR, but not macroalbuminuria, with effects sustained only at the three-month follow-up. The researchers suggest that the lack of change in dicarbonyl detoxification and DNA-damage markers may explain the relapse of albuminuria.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The study randomized 38 patients with type 2 diabetes and diabetic nephropathy into a fasting-mimicking diet or Mediterranean diet group. The FMD involved specific caloric and macronutrient compositions for five consecutive days each month, while the M-Diet maintained caloric intake. Primary and secondary endpoints included changes in ACR, HOMA-IR, and various metabolic markers, with statistical analysis performed using ANCOVA on the intention-to-treat population.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The study found that the fasting-mimicking diet reduced microalbuminuria and improved metabolic control in type 2 diabetes patients, but these effects were transient and did not alter macroalbuminuria. The diet led to a reduction in antihyperglycemic and antihypertensive medication use, and increased blood ketones, while maintaining comparable glycemic and blood pressure control to the Mediterranean diet group. The researchers attribute the transient nature of the albuminuria reduction to the lack of sustained changes in dicarbonyl detoxification and DNA-damage repair markers.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The study suggests that the transient nature of albuminuria reduction is due to a lack of sustained changes in dicarbonyl detoxification and DNA-damage repair markers, indicating that longer fasting-mimicking diet periods may be necessary for nephropathy reversal. The research highlights the clinical feasibility of integrating FMD into diabetes care, noting that the reduction in albuminuria was significant only in the subgroup of patients with microalbuminuria. The authors caution that the small sample size and the lack of renal biopsy data limit the generalizability and mechanistic understanding of the findings.
